etymology: A blend of stay and vacation: time off spent at home or nearby instead of travelling. Scattered uses appear in the early 2000s; the word took off in 2008, when high gas prices and the financial crisis kept families close to home, and Merriam-Webster added it in 2009. It returned in force during the travel restrictions of 2020. Variants: daycation, nearcation.
biblical_def: A staycation is a vacation without the travel: days off spent at home, sleeping in, exploring the local museum, grilling in the backyard, or doing nothing in particular. It began as a recession necessity and became, for many, a preference. The Christian observation: the staycation is a small rediscovery of something Scripture built into the week. God commanded rest that required no travel at all: the Sabbath, a day at home before Him. "Six days thou shalt work, but on the seventh day thou shalt rest" (Exo 34:21). The Lord Jesus invited tired disciples, "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while" (Mar 6:31), and the desert place was a boat ride away, not a flight. Scripture also prizes contentment with one’s own place: "Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith" (Pro 15:17). The staycation can teach a family that rest does not need to be purchased far away, and that home can be a place of delight rather than only of chores. Its one caution is that a staycation can become screens all day, which is neither rest nor vacation. A father plans a staycation like a feast: no work email, long meals, walks, games, church on Sunday, a visit to the grandparents, and maybe a night of stargazing in the yard. "Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for the LORD hath dealt bountifully with thee" (Psa 116:7).
webster_summary: Millennial-era slang (2008 recession; Merriam-Webster 2009) for a vacation spent at home; redeemable as a small recovery of Sabbath rest and contentment with one’s own place (Exo 34:21; Psa 116:7).
webster_full: STAYCATION, n. (Millennial-era slang, 2008–present; blend of stay + vacation) A vacation spent at home or near home rather than travelling. Variants: daycation.

Webster (1828), root vacation: VACATION, noun [Latin vacatio.] 1. The act of making void, vacant, or of no validity; as the vacation of a charter. 2. Intermission of judicial proceedings; the space of time between the end of one term and the beginning of the next; non-term. 3. The intermission of the regular studies and exercises of a college or other seminary, when the students have a recess. 4. Intermission of a stated employment. 5. The time when a see or other spiritual dignity is vacant. […]
Decode for parents: plan the staycation like a feast, with screens put away and God thanked.
scriptures: Six days thou shalt work, but on the seventh day thou shalt rest: in earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest.
Mar 6:31
And he said unto them, Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while: for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.
Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.
Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for the LORD hath dealt bountifully with thee.
It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep.
corruption_summary: The staycation is a wholesome recovery of rest at home; its only drift is rest that becomes idle screens rather than renewal before God.
corruption_paragraphs: There is little to correct here. The only drift is that rest at home can become not rest but distraction: a week of streaming and scrolling that leaves everyone more tired. Sabbath rest in Scripture is not mere inactivity; it is delight in God and His gifts, worship, fellowship, and renewal. A staycation without that can be an empty week.

The redemption is to treat home as a place of gladness. "It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late … for so he giveth his beloved sleep" (Psa 127:2). Teach children that they do not need an airport to rest, that their own table and yard can be places of joy, and that the weekly Sabbath is God’s standing staycation, given freely to His people.
roots_summary: Stay + Latin vacatio (freedom from duty) → vacation → early-2000s staycation → 2008 recession popularity → Merriam-Webster 2009.
roots_lines: Latin vacare — to be empty, free; vacatio — freedom from duty
Early 2000s: scattered uses of staycation
2008: recession and gas prices popularize it; 2009: Merriam-Webster
2020: travel restrictions revive it
Biblical anchor: on the seventh day thou shalt rest (Exo 34:21); return unto thy rest, O my soul (Psa 116:7)
usage: "We’re doing a staycation this year: backyard, bikes, and board games."
Come ye yourselves apart … and rest a while (Mar 6:31).
Better is a dinner of herbs where love is (Pro 15:17).

etymology: A blend of glamorous and camping: camping with the comforts of a hotel, in furnished safari tents, yurts, treehouses, or cabins with real beds, electricity, and sometimes room service. The word appeared in Britain about 2005 and spread with Millennial travel culture and Instagram in the 2010s; it entered the major dictionaries during that decade. The older ideal of "roughing it" was turned on its head.
biblical_def: Glamping is camping without the hardship: a canvas tent with a king bed, string lights, a wood stove, and a bathroom, set in a beautiful place and priced like a hotel. The Christian observation: there is nothing wrong with comfortable lodging in a lovely place, and much right with getting families outdoors under God’s sky. "The heavens declare the glory of God" (Psa 19:1), and they are easier to see from a field than a city. Two small reflections are worth making. First, Scripture has its own festival of tent-living, and it was designed to be humble. Israel kept the Feast of Tabernacles by dwelling in booths for seven days, "That your generations may know that I made the children of Israel to dwell in booths, when I brought them out of the land of Egypt" (Lev 23:43). The temporary dwelling was a reminder of dependence and pilgrimage: this world is not our permanent home. Second, some value lies in hardship itself. Roughing it teaches children patience, resourcefulness, and gratitude for a roof. "It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth" (Lam 3:27). Glamping can skip those lessons. A father might take his family glamping for a lovely weekend, and also take his sons on a real camping trip with rain, cold, and burnt food, and teach them both: enjoy comfort with thanks, endure discomfort with cheer, and remember that we are "strangers and pilgrims on the earth" (Heb 11:13), living in tents until the city with foundations.
webster_summary: Millennial travel slang (UK c. 2005; 2010s) for luxury camping; harmless enjoyment of creation, with a reminder that Scripture’s tents were humble pilgrim dwellings (Lev 23:43) and that hardship has its lessons (Lam 3:27).
webster_full: GLAMPING, n. (Millennial travel slang, c. 2005–present; blend of glamorous + camping) Camping with hotel-like comforts: furnished tents, yurts, cabins, beds, electricity.

Webster (1828), root camp: CAMP, noun 1. The ground on which an army pitch their tents, whether for a night or a longer time. 2. The order or arrangement of tents, or disposition of an army, for rest; as, to pitch a camp Also, the troops encamped on the same field. 3. An army.
Decode for parents: enjoy the comfy tent; also give your children a night of real camping and real gratitude.
scriptures: Psa 19:1
The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.
That your generations may know that I made the children of Israel to dwell in booths, when I brought them out of the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.
Lam 3:27
It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
corruption_summary: Glamping is harmless comfort outdoors; its only lesson is that comfort can skip the humility of the tent and the gifts of hardship.
corruption_paragraphs: The slight drift is the removal of every hardship from every experience. A culture that glamps, Ubers, and orders in can raise children who have never been cold, wet, or hungry by choice, and who have not learned the gratitude and resilience those experiences teach. The tents of Scripture were teachers of dependence; a tent with a chandelier teaches something else.

The redemption is to use both. Enjoy beauty and comfort as gifts, and give children the formative gift of a little hardship too. And let the tent, glamorous or not, preach its sermon: "For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens" (2Co 5:1).
roots_summary: Glamour (Scots, a magic spell; then allure) + Latin campus (field) → camp → c. 2005 glamping (UK) → 2010s Millennial travel trend.
roots_lines: Scots glamour — a spell; later, alluring charm
Latin campus — a field → camp — ground where tents are pitched
c. 2005: glamping in Britain
2010s: Instagram-era trend; yurts, safari tents, treehouses
Biblical anchor: I made the children of Israel to dwell in booths (Lev 23:43); strangers and pilgrims (Heb 11:13)
usage: "We went glamping: tent, but with a real bed and a fire pit."
The booths of Israel taught dependence (Lev 23:43).
It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth (Lam 3:27).

etymology: A person with an enthusiastic, refined interest in food. The word appeared about 1980 (the restaurant critic Gael Greene is often credited) and was popularized by The Official Foodie Handbook (1984) by Ann Barr and Paul Levy. Millennials made foodie culture mainstream in the 2000s–2010s: food television, celebrity chefs, food trucks, farm-to-table restaurants, and, above all, photographing meals for Instagram ("the camera eats first").
biblical_def: A foodie loves food, not just to eat it but to seek it out, discuss it, photograph it, and rank it: the new taco truck, the tasting menu, the perfect sourdough. The Christian observation: there is real goodness in this. God made food delicious on purpose; He could have made it merely nourishing. "Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart; for God now accepteth thy works" (Ecc 9:7). The Lord Jesus’ first miracle provided the best wine at a wedding (Joh 2:10), and He was so often at tables that His enemies called Him a glutton. Scripture is full of feasts, and heaven is pictured as a banquet. Careful cooking and grateful eating honour the Giver. But Scripture also names a danger in exactly this area: the belly as god. Paul wept over those "whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things" (Php 3:19). Gluttony is not only overeating; it is an excessive preoccupation with food, the appetite that rules. Esau sold his birthright for a bowl of stew (Gen 25:33-34). The foodie culture can also be a status game, refined taste as a way of looking down on others. A father teaches his children to love good food, to cook it well, to share it generously, and to thank God for it; and to remember that "Meats for the belly, and the belly for meats: but God shall destroy both it and them" (1Co 6:13), while the bread of life endures for ever.
webster_summary: A 1980s coinage made Millennial culture (food TV, Instagram meals) for a food enthusiast; enjoying God’s good food with joy is biblical (Ecc 9:7), but the belly can become a god (Php 3:19).
webster_full: FOODIE, n. (c. 1980; Millennial mainstream, 2000s–2010s) A person with an enthusiastic and discerning interest in food and eating. Culture: food photography, food trucks, tasting menus, "the camera eats first."

Webster (1828), root food: FOOD, noun [ See Feed .] 1. In a general sense, whatever is eaten by animals for nourishment, and whatever supplies nutriment to plants. 2. Meat; aliment; flesh or vegetables eaten for sustaining human life; victuals; provisions; whatever is or may be eaten for nourishment. Feed me with food convenient for me. Proverbs 30:8 . 3. Whatever supplies nourishment and growth to plants, as water, carbonic acid gas, etc. Manuring substances furnish plants with food 4. Something that sustains, nourishes and augments. […]
Decode for parents: teach the joy of good food and the discipline that keeps appetite from ruling.
scriptures: Ecc 9:7
Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart; for God now accepteth thy works.
Joh 2:10
And saith unto him, Every man at the beginning doth set forth good wine; and when men have well drunk, then that which is worse: but thou hast kept the good wine until now.
Php 3:19
Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.)
Then Jacob gave Esau bread and pottage of lentiles; and he did eat and drink, and rose up, and went his way: thus Esau despised his birthright.
Meats for the belly, and the belly for meats: but God shall destroy both it and them. Now the body is not for fornication, but for the Lord; and the Lord for the body.
corruption_summary: Foodie culture rightly delights in God’s good food, but can make the belly a god and taste a status; Scripture commands joyful eating and warns against appetite that rules.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is appetite enthroned. When food becomes identity, hobby, social currency, and the main thing one looks forward to, it has moved from gift to god. Esau is the warning: "Thus Esau despised his birthright" (Gen 25:34), trading the eternal for a meal. The foodie culture’s photographs, rankings, and refined contempt for ordinary food can also make the table a place of pride rather than fellowship.

The recovery is grateful, generous eating. Christians should cook well, eat with joy, and set wide tables; hospitality is commanded, and good food is a fine instrument of it. Teach the young to thank God before every meal, to fast sometimes so that appetite stays a servant, and to remember the One who said, "I am the bread of life."
roots_summary: Old English foda (food) → food + diminutive -ie → c. 1980 foodie → 1984 Official Foodie Handbook → 2000s–2010s Millennial food culture.
roots_lines: Old English foda — food, nourishment
c. 1980: foodie in restaurant criticism
1984: Barr and Levy, The Official Foodie Handbook
2000s–2010s: food TV, Instagram meals, food trucks
Biblical anchor: eat thy bread with joy (Ecc 9:7); whose God is their belly (Php 3:19)
usage: "She’s a total foodie; she knows every taco truck in town."
Eat thy bread with joy (Ecc 9:7), and thank the Giver.
Esau despised his birthright for a meal (Gen 25:34).

etymology: From Instagram, the photo-sharing app launched in October 2010 (its name a blend of instant camera and telegram) and bought by Facebook in 2012. By the mid-2010s Instagrammable described anything visually striking enough to photograph and post: a dish, a wall mural, a café, a wedding, a destination. Businesses began designing for it (neon signs, flower walls, the 2016 Museum of Ice Cream), and travel choices were made by it.
biblical_def: Something is Instagrammable if it will look good in a photo: the pastel café, the rainbow bagel, the cliff at sunset, the wedding with the perfect light. The word reveals a new way of evaluating experiences: by how they will appear to others. The Christian observation: beauty is good, and photographs can preserve real joys. God made a beautiful world, and noticing beauty is a form of praise. But "Instagrammable" quietly shifts the question from "Is this good?" to "Will this look good?" It trains people to value the appearance of a life over its substance, and that is a very old temptation. The Lord Jesus warned against good deeds done "before men, to be seen of them" (Mat 6:1) and against those who "make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess" (Mat 23:25). Scripture’s standard runs the other way: "for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart" (1Sa 16:7). The most important parts of a Christian life are usually not Instagrammable: the hidden prayer, the quiet repentance, the diaper changed at 3 a.m., the visit to a lonely widow. "Thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly" (Mat 6:4). A father can enjoy a beautiful view and take a picture, and he can teach his children to choose their meals, trips, and weddings by what is good, not by what photographs well, and to treasure the unpostable moments most.
webster_summary: Millennial slang (mid-2010s, from Instagram, 2010) for visually striking enough to post; beauty is good, but valuing life by its appearance is the old error of the clean outside of the cup (Mat 23:25; 1Sa 16:7).
webster_full: INSTAGRAMMABLE, adj. (Millennial slang, mid-2010s–present; from Instagram) Visually appealing enough to be photographed and posted on social media. "The café is so Instagrammable."

Webster (1828), root telegraph: TELEGRAPH, noun [Gr. at a distance, and to write.] A machine for communicating intelligence from a distance by various signals or movements previously agreed on; which signals represent letters, words or ideas which can be transmitted form one station to another, as far as the signals can be seen. This machine was invented by the French about the year 1793 or 1794, and is now adopted by other nations.
Decode for parents: ask your children what they would do if no one could see it; that is the real test of a good experience.
scriptures: Mat 6:1
Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven.
Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess.

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
Mat 6:4
That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly.
Ecc 3:11
He hath made every thing beautiful in his time: also he hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end.
corruption_summary: Instagrammable judges experiences by how they appear to others; Scripture looks on the heart and rewards what is done in secret.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is life curated for the camera. Restaurants are designed for photos rather than flavour, weddings are planned for the feed, trips are chosen for backdrops. Over time the habit forms a person who experiences his own life as an audience would, always asking how it looks. That is the outside of the cup, polished while the inside is neglected, and it makes the hidden virtues that God prizes feel worthless because they cannot be posted.

The redemption is to love beauty for God’s sake and to treasure the unseen. "He hath made every thing beautiful in his time" (Ecc 3:11). Christians can photograph beauty gladly and share it as praise. But teach the young to choose things because they are good, to keep many moments unrecorded, and to do the most important things in secret, where the Father sees.
roots_lines: Greek tēle — far off; gramma — a thing written → telegram
October 2010: Instagram launches (instant camera + telegram); 2012: bought by Facebook
Mid-2010s: Instagrammable; venues designed for photos
2016: the Museum of Ice Cream and the "selfie museum" trend
Biblical anchor: to be seen of men (Mat 6:1); the LORD looketh on the heart (1Sa 16:7)
usage: "We picked the restaurant because the neon wall is so Instagrammable."
Ye make clean the outside of the cup (Mat 23:25).
Thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly (Mat 6:4).

etymology: A warning that what follows reveals plot details of a book, film, or show. Spoiler in this sense goes back to a 1971 National Lampoon humour piece by Doug Kenney ("Spoilers") that gave away famous endings; Usenet groups of the early 1980s adopted "spoiler warnings" for discussions of films and shows. Spoiler alert became the standard phrase in the 2000s–2010s age of streaming and binge-watching, when audiences watched the same shows at different times and social media made the ending impossible to avoid (the 2013 "Red Wedding" on Game of Thrones was a famous case).
biblical_def: "Spoiler alert" warns that the ending of a story is about to be revealed, so that those who have not watched yet can look away. It is a small courtesy of the streaming age, and also a sly way to announce a surprising fact ("Spoiler alert: the meeting was cancelled"). The Christian observation: the courtesy is a kindness worth keeping, and it is a good example of loving a neighbour in small things. "Let no man seek his own, but every man another’s wealth" (1Co 10:24). There is also a theological delight hiding in the phrase, because God has given His people the biggest spoiler of all. He has told us how the story ends. "Declaring the end from the beginning" (Isa 46:10) is His habit. The last chapters of the Bible tell us that evil will be judged, that death will be defeated, and that "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying" (Rev 21:4). The disciples were told the ending before the crucifixion and still did not understand; Christians know it after the resurrection. Unlike a ruined movie, this spoiler does not spoil the story; it is what makes the middle bearable. "For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us" (Rom 8:18). A father keeps the spoiler courtesy at home, and he gives his children the great spoiler as often as he can: we know how it ends, and Christ wins.
webster_summary: Millennial streaming-age phrase (from 1971 National Lampoon; Usenet; 2000s–2010s) warning of a revealed ending; a small courtesy, and an opening to the gospel’s great spoiler: God has declared the end, and Christ wins (Isa 46:10; Rev 21:4).
webster_full: SPOILER ALERT, interj. / n. (Millennial streaming-age phrase, 2000s–present; from spoiler, 1971) A warning that plot details or an ending will be revealed. Also used jokingly before announcing any fact.
Webster (1828), root spoiler: SPOILER, noun 1. A plunderer; a pillager; a robber. 2. One that corrupts, mars or renders useless.
Decode for parents: keep the courtesy; and tell your children the great spoiler often.
scriptures: Let no man seek his own, but every man another's wealth.
Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:
Rev 21:4
And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.
Rom 8:18
For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.
These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.
corruption_summary: Spoiler alert is a harmless courtesy; its best use is to remind believers that God has revealed the end of the story, and the ending is glory.
corruption_paragraphs: There is little to correct here; avoiding spoilers is a kindness, and spoiling a story deliberately to annoy someone is a small unkindness. The only drift worth noting is a culture so absorbed in fictional endings that it rarely asks about the real one. People will go to great lengths to protect the surprise of a season finale and give no thought to the end of their own lives.

The redemption is the spoiler that saves. "In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world" (Joh 16:33). Christians read the middle of their stories, the sickness, the setback, the grief, in light of an ending they already know. Teach the young to love good stories, to protect each other’s surprises, and to live with the confidence of people who have read the last page of the Book.
roots_summary: Latin spoliare (to strip, plunder) → spoil → spoiler (plunderer; one who mars) → 1971 plot-revealing spoiler → 1980s Usenet warnings → 2000s spoiler alert.
roots_lines: Latin spoliare — to strip, to plunder; KJV spoilers — raiders
Webster 1828: spoiler — a plunderer; one that corrupts or mars
1971: Doug Kenney, "Spoilers," National Lampoon
1980s: Usenet spoiler warnings; 2000s–2010s: streaming, spoiler alert
Biblical anchor: declaring the end from the beginning (Isa 46:10); God shall wipe away all tears (Rev 21:4)
usage: "Spoiler alert: the butler did it."
God gives the ultimate spoiler: no more death, neither sorrow (Rev 21:4).
Be of good cheer; I have overcome the world (Joh 16:33).

etymology: Initialism for too long; didn’t read, from early-2000s internet forums and Usenet, first as a dismissive reply to a long post, then as a label for a summary placed at the top or bottom of one ("TL;DR: the meeting is moved to Friday"). Reddit made the summary use standard in the 2010s, and dictionaries noted the term by about 2013. Variants: tl;dr, TLDR.
biblical_def: TL;DR means "too long; didn’t read." It began as a brush-off to anyone who wrote more than a screenful, and it became a helpful convention: the one-line summary at the top of a long post. The Christian observation: both uses deserve attention. The summary is a real service, and Scripture loves brevity. "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise" (Pro 10:19). "Let thy words be few" (Ecc 5:2). The Lord Jesus summarized the whole law in two commandments (Mat 22:37-40), the greatest TL;DR ever given. But the dismissive use reveals a cultural problem that matters for Christians: shrinking attention. A generation trained on short posts finds long reading hard, and the Bible is long. Its deepest treasures require sustained attention. When Ezra read the Law to the people, "he read therein … from the morning until midday … and the ears of all the people were attentive unto the book of the law" (Neh 8:3). The blessed man’s "delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night" (Psa 1:2). The Bereans "searched the scriptures daily" (Act 17:11). A Christian cannot live on summaries of God’s Word. A father teaches his children to write clearly and briefly, to read slowly and deeply, and to treat the Bible as the one book that is never TL;DR, because every word of it is breath from God.
webster_summary: Millennial internet initialism (early 2000s; Reddit summaries 2010s) for too long; didn’t read; brevity is biblical (Ecc 5:2), but shrinking attention threatens the deep reading Scripture requires (Neh 8:3; Psa 1:2).
webster_full: TL;DR, interj. / n. (Millennial internet slang, early 2000s–present; initialism of too long; didn’t read) (1) A dismissive reply to a long text. (2) A brief summary of a longer text. Also TLDR.

Webster (1828), root read: READ, verb transitive The preterit and participle passive read is pronounced red. [Gr. to say or tell, to flow; a speaker, a rhetorician. The primary sense of read is to speak, to utter, that is, to push, drive or advance. This is also the primary sense of ready, that is, prompt or advancing, quick. Latin gratia, the primary sense of which is prompt to favor, advancing towards, free. The elements of these words are the same as those of ride and Latin gradior, etc. […]
Decode for parents: teach clear summaries and long attention; the Bible needs the second.
scriptures: In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise.
Ecc 5:2
Be not rash with thy mouth, and let not thine heart be hasty to utter any thing before God: for God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few.

Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.
Neh 8:3

And he read therein before the street that was before the water gate from the morning until midday, before the men and the women, and those that could understand; and the ears of all the people were attentive unto the book of the law.
Psa 1:2
But his delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night.
corruption_summary: TL;DR rightly prizes brevity, but its dismissive form signals shrinking attention, which starves the deep, daily reading that Scripture asks of believers.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is attention trained for scraps. The digital world rewards the short, the punchy, and the summarized, and many young people now struggle to read anything long. That is not a neutral change for Christians, who are people of a long Book, written with genealogies, laws, poems, letters, and prophecies that unfold only to patient readers. A faith fed only on verse-of-the-day snippets will be thin.

The recovery is the discipline of deep reading. Read whole books of the Bible aloud as a family; memorize passages, not only verses; read good long books. Ezra’s congregation stood for half a day to hear the Law, and they wept and rejoiced. Teach the young to summarize well for others, and to refuse summaries of the Word of God for themselves.
roots_summary: Old English raedan (to advise, interpret, read) → read → early-2000s forums TL;DR → 2010s Reddit summary label → dictionaries c. 2013.
roots_lines: Old English raedan — to advise, to explain, to read
Early 2000s: forum and Usenet TL;DR — dismissive reply
2010s: Reddit summary convention "TL;DR:"
c. 2013: noted by dictionaries
Biblical anchor: let thy words be few (Ecc 5:2); in his law doth he meditate day and night (Psa 1:2)
usage: "TL;DR: practice is moved to Thursday."
Christ’s TL;DR of the law: love God, love neighbour (Mat 22:37-40).
Ezra read from the morning until midday, and the people listened (Neh 8:3).

etymology: Initialism for for the win, from the television game show Hollywood Squares, where contestants would say "I’ll take [celebrity] for the win." Online gamers and forum users of the 2000s adopted FTW as an exclamation of enthusiastic approval: "Pizza FTW!" "Team Rocket FTW!" (An unrelated, vulgar older initialism uses the same letters; the Millennial sense is the game-show one.) Its opposite, FTL (for the loss), was less common.
biblical_def: FTW means "for the win": an exclamation that something is the best, the winner, the clinching answer. "Grandma’s apple pie FTW." It is enthusiastic, light, and usually harmless. The Christian observation: the word is a cheer, and Scripture is full of cheering for a victory, though of a different kind. The believer’s great "for the win" is not his own: "But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ" (1Co 15:57). The decisive win has already been secured by Christ’s death and resurrection: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" (1Co 15:55). And Christians are called to live as those who run to win: "So run, that ye may obtain" (1Co 9:24); "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith" (2Ti 4:7). There is a caution about the competitive spirit the phrase can carry, the need to win at everything, to be the best, to beat others. Paul ranked godly ambition high and selfish ambition low: "Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory" (Php 2:3). A father teaches his children to play to win, to cheer enthusiastically for good things, and to remember that the only "for the win" that matters eternally belongs to Christ, who gives His victory to those who trust Him.
webster_summary: Millennial internet initialism (2000s, from game-show "for the win") of enthusiastic approval; harmless cheer, pointing to the victory God gives through Christ (1Co 15:57) and the race run to win (1Co 9:24).
webster_full: FTW, interj. (Millennial internet and gaming slang, 2000s–present; initialism of for the win, from Hollywood Squares) Expresses enthusiastic approval of something as the best. "Snow days FTW!"

Webster (1828), root win: WIN, verb transitive preterit tense and participle passive won. [G.] 1. To gain by success in competition or contest; as, to win the prize in a game; to win money; to win a battle, or to win a country. Battles are won by superior strength or skill. --Who thus shall Canaan win 2. To gain by solicitation or courtship. 3. To obtain; to allure to kindness or compliance. Thy virtue won me. win your enemy by kindness. 4. To gain by persuasion or influence; as, an orator wins his audience by argument. […]
Decode for parents: harmless cheer; teach the difference between godly zeal and the need to beat everyone.
scriptures: But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?
Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain.
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
Php 2:3
Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
corruption_summary: FTW is a harmless cheer; its only shadow is a win-at-all-costs spirit, while Scripture’s great victory is Christ’s, given to those who trust Him.
corruption_paragraphs: There is little to correct in the word. If there is a drift, it is the competitive temper of the culture it came from, where everything is a contest and every opinion a team. That spirit can make friendships into rivalries and conversations into battles to be won. Paul’s rule cuts against it: do nothing through strife or vainglory, and esteem others better than yourself.

The redemption is to aim the cheer. Christians can be the most enthusiastic people in any room, because they know the outcome of the great contest. Teach the young to compete wholeheartedly and graciously, to celebrate good things freely, and to rejoice above all that "we are more than conquerors through him that loved us."
roots_summary: Old English winnan (to strive, to gain) → win → Hollywood Squares "for the win" → 2000s gaming and forum FTW.
roots_lines: Old English winnan — to labour, to strive, to gain
Hollywood Squares: "I’ll take [name] for the win"
2000s: gaming and forum initialism FTW
Opposite: FTL, "for the loss"
Biblical anchor: thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory (1Co 15:57)
usage: "Saturday pancakes FTW."
O death, where is thy sting? (1Co 15:55): Christ FTW.
So run, that ye may obtain (1Co 9:24).

etymology: Initialism for in real life, from 1980s–90s Usenet and chat rooms, distinguishing the offline world from online identities and interactions ("we met IRL at the convention"). It became everyday Millennial speech in the 2000s–2010s as more of life moved online. In 2011 the sociologist Nathan Jurgenson criticized "digital dualism," the idea that online life is not real life, arguing that the two are now intertwined; but IRL remains the common way to mark embodied, face-to-face reality.
biblical_def: IRL means "in real life": offline, in person, with bodies in the same room. "We’ve been texting for months, but we finally met IRL." The Christian observation: the phrase carries a quiet truth that Christians should cherish, and a danger they should avoid. The truth: embodied presence matters, and the Christian faith is profoundly IRL. "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us" (Joh 1:14). The apostles insisted on the physical reality of what they had witnessed: "That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the Word of life" (1Jn 1:1). The resurrection was IRL: "handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have" (Luk 24:39). The Lord’s Supper, baptism, and the gathered church are IRL; no screen can replace them. The danger is the implication that online is not real, so online behaviour does not count. Many people say online what they would never say IRL, or pursue online sins they would never commit in person. But God sees both, and our words online are as real as our words aloud: "by thy words thou shalt be justified" (Mat 12:37). A father prizes IRL time with his children, at table and in church, and teaches them that there is only one life, lived before one God, whether the screen is on or off.
webster_summary: Millennial chat initialism (1980s–90s; everyday 2000s–2010s) for in real life, offline; redeemable as a confession that embodied presence matters, as in the Word made flesh (Joh 1:14), so long as online life is not treated as unaccountable (Mat 12:37).
webster_full: IRL, adv. / adj. (Millennial chat and internet slang, 1980s–present; initialism of in real life) Offline; in person; in the physical world. "We met IRL."

Webster (1828), root real: REAL, adjective [Low Latin realis. The Latin res and Eng. thing coincide exactly with the Heb. a word, a thing, an event. See Read and Thing .] 1. Actually being or existing; not fictitious or imaginary; as a description of real life. The author describes a real scene or transaction. 2. True; genuine; not artificial, counterfeit or factitious; as real Madeira wine; real ginger. 3. True; genuine; not affected; not assumed. The woman appears in her real character. 4. Relating to things, not to persons; not personal. […]
Decode for parents: prize IRL time, and teach that online life is just as real before God.
scriptures: Joh 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and our hands have handled, of the Word of life;
Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have.
For by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned.
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
corruption_summary: IRL rightly prizes embodied presence, the faith of the Word made flesh; its danger is treating online life as unreal and unaccountable, when God sees one life.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is digital dualism as a moral holiday. If online is "not real life," then online cruelty, lust, and lies seem not to count, and many young people live double lives: decent IRL, something else on the screen. But God does not grade on two scales. The sin committed in a browser is committed by a real person before a real God. The opposite error is also real: treating online connection as a full substitute for presence, so that church becomes a livestream and friendship becomes a chat.

The redemption is incarnational living. Christians follow a Lord who came in the flesh, rose in the flesh, and will return in the flesh; their worship gathers bodies around Word and sacrament. "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together" (Heb 10:25). Teach the young to choose IRL presence whenever they can, to bring the same integrity to the screen that they bring to the room, and to remember that there is only one life to live faithfully.
roots_summary: Latin res (thing) → realis → real → 1980s–90s chat initialism IRL → 2000s–2010s everyday speech; 2011 "digital dualism" debate.
roots_lines: Latin res — a thing; realis — actual, pertaining to things
1980s–90s: Usenet and chat IRL
2000s–2010s: everyday Millennial speech
2011: Nathan Jurgenson’s critique of "digital dualism"
Biblical anchor: the Word was made flesh (Joh 1:14); our hands have handled (1Jn 1:1)
usage: "We’re finally meeting IRL this weekend."
Handle me, and see (Luk 24:39): the resurrection was IRL.
By thy words thou shalt be justified (Mat 12:37), typed or spoken.

etymology: Two roots meet in the internet troll. One is the fishing verb to troll, to drag a baited line behind a slow boat to see what bites; the other is the monster of Norse folklore who lurks under bridges. On Usenet in the late 1980s and early 1990s, "trolling for newbies" meant posting bait to provoke a reaction. By the 2000s a troll was a person who posts deliberately inflammatory, insulting, or off-topic messages to upset others for amusement; trolling became a pervasive online behaviour and, in the 2010s, a political and harassment tactic.
biblical_def: A troll is a person who provokes others online for fun: posting outrageous opinions he may not hold, insulting strangers, derailing conversations, and enjoying the anger that follows. To troll is to fish for reactions with bait. The Christian observation: Scripture describes the troll with uncomfortable precision and calls him wicked. "As coals are to burning coals, and wood to fire; so is a contentious man to kindle strife" (Pro 26:21). Among the seven things the LORD hates is "he that soweth discord among brethren" (Pro 6:19). The man who deceives his neighbour and says "Am not I in sport?" is like a madman with firebrands (Pro 26:18-19). Trolling is a sin of the tongue, often several at once: lying, mockery, contention, and cruelty for entertainment. Scripture also gives wisdom for the trolled. "Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like unto him" (Pro 26:4); sometimes the wisest response is silence. Paul tells Timothy, "But foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes. And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men" (2Ti 2:23-24). And for persistent troublemakers in the church: "A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject" (Tit 3:10). A father tells his children: never troll anyone, not even as a joke, because the person on the other end is real; and when you are trolled, do not take the bait. The troll wants your anger; give him silence or kindness instead.
webster_summary: Millennial internet slang (late 1980s Usenet; fishing troll + Norse monster) for one who provokes others online for amusement; Scripture calls him a sower of discord whom the LORD hates (Pro 6:19; 26:21) and counsels not answering the fool (Pro 26:4). Reject.
webster_full: TROLL, n. / v. (internet slang, late 1980s; Millennial mainstream, 2000s–present) A person who posts inflammatory or insulting messages to provoke others; to provoke in this way. Also trolling, troll farm.
Webster (1828), root troll: TROLL, verb intransitive To roll; to run about; as, to troll in a coach and six. 1. Among anglers, to fish for pikes with a rod whose line runs on a wheel or pulley.
Decode for parents: ask your children if they have ever trolled someone "as a joke," and if they have been trolled; teach them not to take the bait.
scriptures: As coals are to burning coals, and wood to fire; so is a contentious man to kindle strife.
Pro 6:19
A false witness that speaketh lies, and he that soweth discord among brethren.
Pro 26:4
Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou also be like unto him.
But foolish and unlearned questions avoid, knowing that they do gender strifes. And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient,
Tit 3:10
A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject;
corruption_summary: Trolling makes provocation entertainment; Scripture names the contentious man and the sower of discord as hated by God, and teaches the trolled not to take the bait.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is cruelty for sport. Trolling turns other people into fish to be hooked for the pleasure of watching them thrash. It has poisoned online life, driven people from public conversation, and in its organized forms spread lies on a vast scale. Many young men have learned to troll as a hobby, and some have grown into it as a personality. Scripture’s verdict is not that trolls are annoying but that they are wicked: they kindle strife and sow discord, and God hates it.

The recovery is a governed tongue and a refusal of the bait. "Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out" (Pro 26:20). Christians should never troll, and should rarely feed trolls; answer once in truth if needed, then walk away. Teach the young that every screen name is a soul, that provoking people is not humour, and that the gentle answer and the silent pass are signs of strength.
roots_summary: Old French troller (to wander) / angling troll (drag a baited line) + Old Norse troll (monster) → late-1980s Usenet "trolling for newbies" → 2000s troll → 2010s troll farms.
roots_lines: Old French troller — to wander; Webster 1828: among anglers, to fish with a running line
Old Norse troll — a giant, a monster under the bridge
Late 1980s–early 1990s: Usenet "trolling for newbies"
2000s–2010s: troll as person; trolling as harassment and propaganda
Biblical anchor: he that soweth discord among brethren (Pro 6:19); answer not a fool according to his folly (Pro 26:4)
usage: "Don’t feed the trolls."
As coals are to burning coals … so is a contentious man to kindle strife (Pro 26:21).
The servant of the Lord must not strive (2Ti 2:24).

etymology: A person who is aggressive, brave, or combative only online, where he can attack from behind a screen and often a pseudonym, but who would not say the same things face to face. The phrase (with variants keyboard commando, keyboard cowboy, keyboard tough guy) circulated on internet forums in the 2000s and became common in the 2010s for online bullies, armchair critics, and those who fight culture-war battles exclusively in comment sections.
biblical_def: A keyboard warrior is fierce online and quiet everywhere else: the man who blasts strangers in comment sections, threatens and insults behind a username, wages crusades in replies, and would never say any of it to a face. The Christian observation: the phrase identifies a combination of two sins, cruelty and cowardice, and Scripture rebukes both. The cruelty is the unbridled tongue: "If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this man’s religion is vain" (Jas 1:26). "A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards" (Pro 29:11). The cowardice is the distance. Scripture expects grievances to be handled in person, face to face: "go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone" (Mat 18:15). Boldness in the Bible is costly and in the open; Paul "withstood him to the face" when Peter erred (Gal 2:11). The keyboard warrior has the courage of anonymity, which is not courage at all. Many Christians are tempted here, especially in theological and political arguments, and the cost is great: "Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice" (Eph 4:31). A father tells his son: never type what you would not say to the man’s face, in front of your pastor and your mother. If something must be confronted, do it in person, with courage and love. Real warriors fight with their names on.
webster_summary: Millennial internet slang (2000s–2010s) for one who is combative only behind a screen; Scripture rebukes both the unbridled tongue (Jas 1:26) and the cowardice of distance, calling for face-to-face confrontation (Mat 18:15; Gal 2:11). Reject.
webster_full: KEYBOARD WARRIOR, n. (Millennial internet slang, 2000s–present) A person who is aggressive or combative online but not in person. Variants: keyboard commando, keyboard cowboy, keyboard tough guy.
Webster (1828), root warrior: WARRIOR, noun 1. In a general sense, a soldier; a man engaged in military life. 2. Emphatically, a brave man; a good soldier.
Decode for parents: "Would you say it to his face?" is the test for every post.
scriptures: Jas 1:26
If any man among you seem to be religious, and bridleth not his tongue, but deceiveth his own heart, this man's religion is vain.
A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards.
Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.
Gal 2:11
But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed.
Eph 4:31
Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice:
corruption_summary: The keyboard warrior combines a cruel tongue with the cowardice of distance; Scripture bridles the tongue and requires confrontation face to face, with love.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is courage counterfeited. The screen removes the costs that normally restrain speech: the other man’s face, the social consequence, the possibility of being answered in person. What remains is the pleasure of attacking without risk. Many young men discover in comment sections a version of themselves that is bolder and nastier than they would ever be IRL, and they mistake it for strength. It is the opposite. Proverbs calls the uncontrolled mouth a fool’s.

The recovery is real courage, which is embodied and accountable. Christians should be willing to say hard truths, and to say them to people’s faces, with their names attached, in love. Teach the young to post only what they would say in person, to take disagreements offline when they matter, and to aim their warrior instincts at their own sin and at serving others. The bravest thing most keyboard warriors could do is log off and make a phone call.
roots_summary: Old French guerreor (warrior) + keyboard → 2000s forum slang keyboard warrior → 2010s comment-section culture.
roots_lines: Old North French werreior / Old French guerreor — a fighter
2000s: forum slang keyboard warrior, keyboard commando
2010s: comment-section and social-media combat; anonymity
Related: troll, armchair critic
Biblical anchor: bridleth not his tongue (Jas 1:26); I withstood him to the face (Gal 2:11)
usage: "He’s a keyboard warrior; online he’s fearless, in person he won’t make eye contact."
Tell him his fault between thee and him alone (Mat 18:15).
A fool uttereth all his mind (Pro 29:11).

etymology: Modelled on midlife crisis (coined 1965 by the psychologist Elliott Jaques), the phrase names a period of anxiety and doubt in one’s twenties about career, relationships, identity, and direction. It was popularized by Alexandra Robbins and Abby Wilner’s book Quarterlife Crisis (2001) and became a defining Millennial experience after the 2008 recession, when many graduates faced debt, underemployment, and delayed milestones.
biblical_def: A quarter-life crisis is the anxious season in one’s twenties: the degree did not lead where it promised, friends are marrying or moving, the job is unsatisfying, and the question "what am I doing with my life?" will not go away. For Millennials, who came of age with student debt and a recession, it became a shared experience. The Christian observation: the questions are good questions, and they often come at the right time. Scripture addresses the young directly: "Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not" (Ecc 12:1). The twenties are meant to be a season of seeking God’s direction and taking up responsibility: "It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth" (Lam 3:27). The crisis often arises because a generation was told that it could be anything and that fulfilment would come from self-discovery and the perfect career. Scripture gives a steadier foundation. Identity comes from God, not achievement; direction comes from Him step by step: "A man’s heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps" (Pro 16:9). Fulfilment comes from faithfulness in ordinary callings: work, marriage, children, church, neighbour. The young are not to wait for certainty before obeying: "Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers" (1Ti 4:12). A father tells his son or daughter in the middle of a quarter-life crisis: you do not need to see the whole road; take the next faithful step, trust the Lord with the rest, and do not waste these years waiting to feel ready.
webster_summary: Millennial term (book 2001; post-2008 surge) for anxiety and doubt in one’s twenties about direction and identity; good questions, best answered by remembering the Creator in youth (Ecc 12:1) and taking the next faithful step (Pro 16:9).
webster_full: QUARTER-LIFE CRISIS, n. (Millennial term, 2001–present; after midlife crisis) A period of anxiety, uncertainty, and self-questioning in one’s twenties regarding career, relationships, and purpose.

Webster (1828), root crisis: CRISIS, noun plural [Gr. Latin , to separate, to determine, to decide. See Crime .] 1. In medical science, the change of a disease which indicates its event; that change which indicates recovery or death. It is sometimes used to designate the excretion of something noxious from the body, or of the noxious fluids in a fever. 2. The decisive state of things, or the point of time when an affair is arrive to its highth, and must soon terminate or suffer a material change. This hours the very crisis of your fate.
Decode for parents: meet your twenty-something’s crisis with patience, Scripture, and the next concrete step.
scriptures: Ecc 12:1
Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them;
Lam 3:27
It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.
Pro 16:9
A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.
Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
The steps of a good man are ordered by the LORD: and he delighteth in his way.
corruption_summary: The quarter-life crisis asks good questions but often rests on the false promise of self-made identity and perfect fulfilment; Scripture roots identity in God and direction in faithful steps.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption lies in the expectations behind the crisis. Millennials were told that they were special, that they should follow their passion, and that the right career would complete them. When reality disappointed, many concluded something had gone wrong with their lives, rather than with the promise. The result was paralysis: postponing marriage, commitment, and vocation until certainty arrived, which it never does.

The recovery is ordinary faithfulness under God’s guidance. "The steps of a good man are ordered by the LORD: and he delighteth in his way" (Psa 37:23). Teach the young that the twenties are not for finding themselves but for giving themselves: to God, to work, to a spouse, to a church, to neighbours. Purpose is found along the way of obedience, not before it. The crisis can then become a turning point toward the Creator they were made to remember.
roots_summary: Greek krisis (decision, judgment) → crisis + quarter-life (after Jaques’s midlife crisis, 1965) → 2001 Quarterlife Crisis → post-2008 Millennial experience.
roots_lines: Greek krinein — to separate, to decide; krisis — a turning point
1965: Elliott Jaques coins midlife crisis
2001: Robbins and Wilner, Quarterlife Crisis
Post-2008: debt, underemployment, delayed milestones
Biblical anchor: remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth (Ecc 12:1); the LORD directeth his steps (Pro 16:9)
usage: "Twenty-six, new job, no idea what I’m doing. Quarter-life crisis."
It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth (Lam 3:27).
A man’s heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps (Pro 16:9).

etymology: An adult child who moves back into the parental home after a period of independence, typically after college, a job loss, or a breakup, as a boomerang returns to the thrower. The phrase and its collective form, boomerang generation, date from the 1980s–90s but became bywords for Millennials after the 2008 recession. In 2016 the Pew Research Center reported that, for the first time in more than 130 years, living with parents was the most common arrangement for Americans aged 18 to 34.
biblical_def: A boomerang kid is a grown child who returns to live with his parents after leaving: back in the childhood bedroom at twenty-five, sometimes for a few months, sometimes for years. For Millennials, facing student debt and a hard job market, it became common enough to name a generation. The Christian observation: the arrangement itself is not shameful, and Scripture is gentler about it than modern culture is. For most of history, adult children lived near or with their parents, and multigenerational households are normal in the Bible. Families are supposed to help: "But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith" (1Ti 5:8). The most famous boomerang kid in Scripture is the prodigal son, and his father ran to meet him (Luk 15:20). But Scripture also expects grown children to grow up. "Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife" (Gen 2:24): the leaving is part of becoming a man. Paul expects everyone to work: "that with quietness they work, and eat their own bread" (2Th 3:12). The question is whether the return is a season of help on the way to responsibility, or a retreat from it. A father welcomes his boomerang son home, gives him a room and a key, and also gives him chores, rent if he can pay it, a plan, and a timeline. Home should be a launching pad, not a hiding place, and a son who honours his parents contributes to the household he shares.
webster_summary: Millennial-era term (1980s–90s; post-2008 byword; Pew 2016) for an adult child who moves back home; Scripture honours family help (1Ti 5:8) and the father who runs to the returning son (Luk 15:20), while expecting leaving, work, and responsibility (Gen 2:24; 2Th 3:12).
webster_full: BOOMERANG KID, n. (1980s–present; Millennial byword after 2008) An adult child who returns to live with his or her parents after a period of independence. Collective: boomerang generation.
No Webster 1828 entry located for the root boomerang, an Australian Aboriginal word that entered English only in the 1820s.
Decode for parents: make home a launching pad, with welcome, chores, a plan, and a timeline.
scriptures: But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.
And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.
Gen 2:24
Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
Now them that are such we command and exhort by our Lord Jesus Christ, that with quietness they work, and eat their own bread.
Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
corruption_summary: The boomerang kid can be a season of family help or a retreat from adulthood; Scripture welcomes the returning child and expects leaving, work, and contribution.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption, when there is one, is not the return but the stall. A comfortable childhood bedroom, free meals, and unlimited screens can make it easy to delay work, marriage, and responsibility indefinitely. Parents, fearing conflict, sometimes enable it. Meanwhile the culture mocks the arrangement, which can push young adults into shame rather than growth. Neither the stall nor the shame is biblical.

The recovery is household life with honour and expectation. "Honour thy father and thy mother" (Exo 20:12) includes contributing to their home as an adult. Parents can welcome children back as the prodigal’s father did, and also set clear expectations of work, contribution, and direction. Teach the young that living at home can be a wise season, and that its purpose is to help them launch into their own households and callings.
roots_summary: Dharuk (Aboriginal Australian) bumarit → English boomerang (1820s) → 1980s–90s boomerang kid / generation → post-2008 Millennial byword → Pew 2016.

Post-2008: Millennials returning home amid debt and recession

Biblical anchor: his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran (Luk 15:20); work, and eat their own bread (2Th 3:12)
usage: "After the layoff he moved back home. Boomerang kid."
When he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion (Luk 15:20).
That with quietness they work, and eat their own bread (2Th 3:12).
